title: What Is the $27.40 Rule? Saving $10,000 a Year, Explained
description: The $27.40 rule means saving $27.40 a day to reach about $10,000 in a year. Here is the math, who it fits, and smaller versions that work too.

paa.question: What is the $27.40 rule?
paa.answer: The $27.40 rule is a savings habit: put away $27.40 every day and after 365 days you have about $10,001. It turns a large yearly goal into a small daily one. In practice that is about $384 every two weeks or $833 a month, so it only works if your budget has that much room.

bodyHtml:
The $27.40 rule spread on social media because the math is tidy. Ten thousand dollars divided by 365 days is about $27.40, so saving that amount each day gets you to $10,001 by the end of the year. It is a framing trick more than a budgeting system, and a useful one, as long as you check that your budget can actually carry it.

Where the Number Comes From

Ten thousand divided by 365 is 27.397. Rounded up to $27.40 and multiplied back by 365, it gives $10,001. Some versions use $27.39, which lands a few dollars short of the goal. The point is the same: a five-figure goal feels out of reach, while a daily amount close to the price of a takeout lunch feels doable.

What It Means Per Paycheck

Nobody actually moves $27.40 a day, so convert it to how you are paid.

  • Weekly: $27.40 times 7 is $191.80 a paycheck.
  • Every two weeks: $27.40 times 14 is $383.60 a paycheck.
  • Twice a month: about $416.75 a paycheck.
  • Monthly: about $833.40.

Seen this way, the rule asks for about $833 a month. On a $4,000 monthly take-home pay that is about 21% of income, right around the savings share most budgets aim for. On $2,500 a month it is a third of your pay, which is not realistic for most people.

Who It Fits, and Who It Does Not

It fits someone whose bills are comfortably covered and whose money leaks out in small daily purchases. Turning those into a daily savings target makes the trade-off visible: the $6 coffee and the $12 lunch are now competing with a number you care about.

It does not fit someone whose budget is already tight, someone carrying high-interest card debt, or someone with no emergency fund who might need the money next month. In those cases a $27.40 daily goal can lead to pulling money back out, or to putting regular bills on a card while the savings account looks healthy.

Smaller Versions That Still Work

The structure scales. Saving $5.48 a day gives about $2,000 in a year, which covers a starter emergency fund with room left over. Saving $13.70 a day gives about $5,000. Pick the yearly goal first, divide by 365, and check the per-paycheck figure against what your bills leave behind.

If the money is for a specific goal, our guide on saving for a big purchase without going into debt shows how to set a deadline and a monthly target together.

How to Make It Stick

Automate it. Set a transfer for the day after each payday in the per-paycheck amount above rather than relying on a daily habit. Put the money in a separate savings account, ideally one that earns interest, so it is not sitting next to your spending money.

Before you commit, check that the transfer will not leave you short before the next payday. Forgenta forecasts your balance to payday with your bills on it, which makes it easy to see whether $384 every two weeks fits or whether a smaller version is the honest choice.

If you are saving toward several things at once, our guide on prioritizing multiple savings goals helps decide what gets funded first.

The $27.40 Rule Compared to Other Money Rules

Social media is full of round-number rules, and they solve different problems. The 50/30/20 rule tells you how to split a whole paycheck between needs, wants and savings. The 70/20/10 rule is a similar split with a smaller savings share. The $27.40 rule does neither. It only says how fast you need to save to reach one specific goal.

That makes it a good companion to a budget rather than a replacement for one. Use a split rule to decide how much of your pay can go to savings at all, then use a daily figure like $27.40 to see how long a particular goal will take at that pace. If the split leaves you $500 a month for savings, $27.40 a day is out of reach, but $16.44 a day, about $6,000 a year, is not.

There is also a motivational side. A daily figure gives you something to beat. Some people track it on a calendar, marking each day they stayed within plan, which turns an abstract yearly goal into a visible streak.

Interest helps a little at the edges. Money that sits in a savings account earning several percent a year grows while you add to it, so the last few months of the year need slightly less from you than the first. It is a bonus, not a strategy, but it is one more reason not to keep the savings in checking.

Whatever daily figure you choose, review it every three months. If the transfers have gone through without strain, raise the amount a little. If you have had to pull money back out, lower it to a level you can hold, because a steady smaller habit outperforms a large one that keeps breaking. The rule is a tool for momentum, and momentum comes from a number you can keep hitting.

The Bottom Line

The $27.40 rule is a simple way to make $10,000 a year feel reachable: about $833 a month or $384 every two weeks. Use it if your budget has that room. If it does not, keep the idea and shrink the number, because a smaller goal you keep beats a large one you abandon in March.

faqs.q: How much is $27.40 a day per month?
faqs.a: About $833. Multiply $27.40 by 365 days and divide by 12 months.
For people with about $833 a month left after bills, yes. For tighter budgets, a smaller daily amount with the same method works better.

faqs.q: Where should I keep the money?
faqs.a: In a separate savings account that earns interest, away from your everyday checking account so it is not spent by accident.
